pages.title: Applied Materials opens $5 billion EPIC Center to speed up AI-era chip development
pages.text:
Applied Materials opens $5 billion EPIC Center to speed up AI-era chip development
The Sunnyvale facility brings TSMC, Intel, Samsung and others under one roof to cut chip development cycles by at least 30%
Silicon Valley is home to companies worth trillions of dollars apiece. Apple, Alphabet and Meta all live there.
What the region has rarely had is the heavy industrial machinery behind those fortunes. Most chip facilities now operate overseas or in other states, and the local skyline is mostly modest office parks.
Applied Materials is trying to change that. On October 12, 2026, the company inaugurated its $5 billion Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization (EPIC) Center in Sunnyvale, California.
The facility is described as the largest investment in advanced semiconductor R&D in the United States.
The building covers 600,000 square feet. Nearly four acres of that is cleanroom space, the ultra-controlled environment where chip processes are developed and tested.
Construction took more than six million hours of labor.
The headline goal is speed. Applied Materials aims to shrink the traditional semiconductor development cycle by at least 30%.
The mechanism is collaboration. Today, the path from a new chipmaking idea to a working production process tends to move step by step. An equipment maker builds a tool, a chipmaker tests it, researchers study the results, and the loop repeats.
The EPIC Center is designed to run those steps in parallel. Chipmakers, equipment manufacturers and academic researchers can work on the same problems at the same site, at the same time.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
The work is also aimed far down the road. The center focuses on technologies three to four generations ahead of what is in production today.
The partner list reads like a who’s who of the global chip industry. Founding partners include TSMC, Intel, SK hynix, Micron and Samsung Electronics.
Broadcom joins as an innovation partner. Stanford and UC Berkeley are among the academic institutions involved.
The facility is also expected to improve access to mature technologies through faster collaboration.
The timing is tied to surging demand for AI capabilities. AI workloads require increasingly complex, high-performance chips, and the industry faces mounting pressure to deliver them faster.
Applied Materials CEO Gary Dickerson has stressed the need for integrated development processes. His argument is that the old, sequential approach cannot keep up with the complexity AI-driven chip demand now requires.
For investors watching the semiconductor sector, the clearest signal is coordination. When TSMC, Intel, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron all sign on as founding partners, it suggests the industry sees shared R&D infrastructure as worth the competitive awkwardness.
If the center delivers on the 30% target, the payoff could be faster time-to-market for advanced chips.
Because the work targets technologies three to four generations ahead of current production, participants may get a head start on processes that competitors outside the partnership will only see later.
For Applied Materials specifically, the move positions the company as more than a toolmaker. It becomes the host of the industry’s shared lab, which could deepen its relationships with the biggest customers in the business.
The things to watch from here: how quickly partner projects move through the facility, whether additional companies or universities join, and whether the promised speedup shows up in actual product roadmaps rather than press materials.

Applied Materials Cratered 20% Since July: Multiple Wall Street Firms Predict It’s Going to More Than Double From Here
Applied Materials just suffered one of its steepest drops in years, yet analysts keep raising their earnings estimates and some price targets sit nearly double the current share price. Here is what the disconnect reveals about where semiconductor equipment spending…
Published October 19, 2026, 7:15am ET · 3 min read
Upward trends on a financial chart overlaid on microchips illustrate the strong performance and growth within the semiconductor market, reflecting the article's focus on chip fund returns. © TechAnimationStock / Shutterstock.com
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT | AMAT Price Prediction) is now priced at $409.29. The average analyst price target stands at $627.83, meaning 53.4% upside.
Applied makes the deposition, etch and inspection tools used to build virtually every new chip. AI infrastructure demand drove fiscal third-quarter revenue to $9.12 billion, up 24.8% year over year. Management guided the current quarter to about $10.25 billion.
The most bullish firms, including H.C. Wainwright and Susquehanna, have $900 targets. Those sit about 119.9% above the current price. Consensus upside stands above 40%.
Investor Day Silence Turned a Pullback Into a 37% Rout
The biggest hit came at Applied’s investor day, when the company declined to provide an industry spending forecast. Shares fell as much as 9% intraday, and the stock lost 19.28% over the past week. Since the start of July, Applied has dropped 37.05%. That leaves it 44.6% below its 52-week high of $738.88.
The first signs showed after the August earnings report. Shares fell about 4% even though guidance beat consensus. Morgan Stanley summed it up: “AMAT’s earnings were good, but not great.” Peers fell about 4% on investor day, so sector weakness made a company-specific hit worse.
33 of 40 Analysts Rate It a Buy as Estimates Climb
Of the 40 analysts who cover Applied, 4 rate it Strong Buy, 29 rate it Buy and 7 rate it Hold. None rate it Sell. Estimates rose while the stock fell. The fiscal 2027 EPS consensus is $18.4672, up from $16.7456 90 days ago. Over the past 30 days, analysts made three upward revisions and no cuts. The stock trades at about 22 times that figure.
Management guided fourth-quarter EPS to about $4.02. DRAM revenue, including HBM packaging, grew 52% year over year. Packaging revenue should grow more than 70% in calendar 2026. Leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging should account for about 80% of equipment growth.
The $900 camp argues that Applied is well placed in tools for Gate-All-Around transistors, backside power and HBM packaging. CEO Gary Dickerson set the timeline on the earnings call: “Based on the unprecedented visibility we’re receiving from our customers, we expect another strong record year in 2027.”
Lam, KLA and Teradyne Sold Off Too, but Applied Fell Hardest
The whole group fell over the past week, but Applied fell the most.
Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) lost 14.74% to $263.94. Its average target is $375.81, meaning 42.4% upside. Twenty-nine of 35 analysts rate it Buy or Strong Buy.
KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) dropped 12.82% to $165.74. Its target of $232.77 meaning 40.4% upside. Analysts are more cautious here, with 10 of 29 at Hold.
Teradyne (NASDAQ:TER) slid 15.33% to $325. Its target of $446.47 meaning 37.4% upside, and 12 of 17 analysts are bullish.
Applied has the largest consensus upside in the group. All of these targets are estimates, and they could fall if spending expectations drop.
A 59.83% Gain This Year Survives the Drawdown
Applied trades at $409.29. The average target from 40 analysts is $627.83, meaning 53.4% upside. Targets often lag sharp price moves, so treat that number as one input among several.
Even after the drop, the stock is up 59.83% year to date. The S&P 500 is up 11.93%. Over one year, Applied shares are up 80.75%.
Applied Materials Looks Like an Overcorrection Worth Researching
Applied Materials’ upside case strengthens if DRAM and leading-edge logic deliver the second-half surge management promised and fiscal 2027 earnings land near the $18.4672 consensus. At a forward P/E of about 23, that growth looks undervalued.
The upside story weakens if the investor day silence means equipment spending is peaking. Management claims multi-year visibility yet held back an industry forecast. China fell to 28% of revenue from 35%, and the Other segment’s loss widened to $118 million. A slowdown in AI capex would pull targets down toward the share price.
The data leans positive. Estimates are rising while the share price falls. Applied’s upside is also the largest of any peer. The next earnings report and its 2027 outlook will test that view. pages.title: Applied Materials vs. Broadcom: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
As the demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to accelerate, investors often weigh the merits of equipment providers against those of chip designers. Choosing between Applied Materials (AMAT -1.97%) and Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%) requires a close look at two very different roles in the global supply chain.
Applied Materials provides the essential tools used to fabricate advanced chips, while Broadcom designs specialized silicon and infrastructure software. They are being compared because both are vital players in the artificial intelligence build-out, though they operate at different stages of the production cycle. This comparison evaluates their financial health and market positioning.
Applied Materials sells the complex machinery that other companies use to build chips, serving major foundries and memory makers. The expansion of global data centers has kept semiconductor stocks at the center of many growth-focused portfolios. Applied Materials maintains a highly concentrated customer base, with two customers accounting for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue in fiscal 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though it includes a deep partnership with Intel (INTC -0.37%) on next-generation manufacturing.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, an increase of 4.4% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $7 billion, which resulted in a net margin of close to 24.7%. This performance highlights the company's steady financial position in its latest annual report, filed for the period ending in late 2025.
As of its October 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.3. The current ratio, which indicates the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, was nearly 2.6. Free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, was approximately $5.7 billion for the fiscal period.
Broadcom provides a mix of specialized chips and infrastructure software. Its chips are essential for cloud data centers and high-end smartphones, while its software segment offers cybersecurity and cloud infrastructure. The company maintains major agreements including a $200 billion memorandum of understanding with Samsung and a $30 billion chip commitment with Apple (AAPL -1.00%).
In fiscal 2025, revenue grew by about 23.9% to nearly $63.9 billion. The company reported net income of approximately $23.1 billion for the year, resulting in a net margin of roughly 36.2%. This was a significant increase in profitability compared to the net income reported in the prior year.
As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.8, while its current ratio was nearly 1.7. Free cash flow reached roughly $26.9 billion for the year. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Applied Materials faces volatility inherent in the semiconductor industry and heavy geographic concentration. Nearly 89% of its revenue comes from outside the United States, making it sensitive to international trade shifts. Complex export controls, particularly regarding sales to China, remain a persistent challenge for the equipment maker. The company also paid a $252 million settlement in 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International.
Broadcom carries substantial indebtedness, which totaled nearly $67.12 billion as of late 2025. Its customer base is also highly concentrated, with a notable reliance on Alphabet for certain revenue streams. The company is navigating intense regulatory scrutiny, including antitrust challenges in the EU related to its VMware operations. Integration risks from large acquisitions and a legal dispute with AT&T (T +0.95%) also factor into its risk profile.
Broadcom is cheaper by forward P/E, which tracks future earnings estimates, while Applied Materials leads on P/S ratio, which measures market cap against 12-month sales.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Broadcom looks kind of expensive to me here. Applied Materials seems relatively boring; 4.4% growth isn't anything to write home about, but I think the valuation reflects that. On the other hand, Broadcom stock has outperformed Applied Materials by over 400 percentage points over the past 10 years, so its elevated valuation may also be justified.
On the other, other hand, smart investors know past performance is no indication of future results, and as a naturally conservative investor, I look at these companies' vastly different market caps and wonder which has the room for more growth. My guess is Applied Materials isn't going to knock your socks off, but it's outpaced the S&P 500 handily over the past 10 years. Furthermore, Broadcom seems closer to a ceiling than Applied Materials; the law of large numbers will make it harder for the former to keep posting those impressive revenue growth rates. I prefer Applied Materials.

Semiconductor Equipment Stocks Slide as Investors Take Profits on a Huge Year: Applied Materials Sinks 7%, Lam Research and KLA Drop 4%
Profit-taking is hammering chipmaking equipment stocks far harder than the broader semiconductor sector, and the gap points to something more specific than a routine pullback after a big year.
Published October 13, 2026, 12:53pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Advanced Microchip illuminated with Red Light in Industrial Environment. Computer Chip on Conveyor Line during Production and Packaging Process on Semiconductor Fab. © Advanced Microchip illuminated with Red Light in Industrial Environment. Computer Chip on Conveyor Line during Production and Packaging Process on Semiconductor Fab. (Shutterstock.com) by IM Imagery
Semiconductor equipment stocks are giving back ground after a strong year powered by artificial intelligence (AI) spending. Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT | AMAT Price Prediction) stock is at $461.91, down 7% in afternoon trading, a pullback that still leaves it up 80% year to date. Selling is greatest among the companies that build chipmaking tools, a narrow corner of the chip trade.
Meanwhile, Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) stock is trading at $297.04, down 4%, a smaller decline than the one hitting Applied Materials stock. Likewise, KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) shares are slipping 4% to $182.44, keeping pace with Lam Research stock.
Chip stocks as a group are holding up far better. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is down 1%. Over in large-cap tech, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 0.5%, a much softer reading than anything in the equipment group.
Applied Materials Gives Back Gains After EPIC Center Debut
Applied Materials stock is giving back part of a large advance, with the decline running alongside its equipment peers. One session earlier, the company unveiled its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization Center, known as the EPIC Center, at its Sunnyvale campus. Management describes the site as the world’s largest facility for collaborative semiconductor process and equipment research. Applied Materials expects capital spending there to scale to approximately $5 billion as customer projects begin.
A leading chipmaker joined the center as a founding partner, giving the project a strong start. Recent results also support the longer-term story. In August, Applied Materials reported Q3 FY2026 adjusted EPS of $3.50 against a $3.39 estimate and guided Q4 FY2026 revenue to about $10.25 billion.
Equipment Makers Slide Harder Than the Broader Chip Group
All three equipment names carry large gains into the pullback, with Lam Research stock up 74% year to date and KLA stock up 51%. Each is falling several times harder than the semiconductor fund that holds them, a split that points at fabrication spending intentions, because the iShares fund also owns chip designers and foundries and its decline serves as broad sector context.
The EPIC Center commits capital to exactly the advanced-node and packaging work that AI buildouts require, and it ties major customers to Applied Materials earlier in the design cycle. In Q3 FY2026, U.S. customers accounted for 15% of Applied Materials’ revenue, while China fell to 28% from 35%. Looking further out, Applied Materials’ chief executive stated in the August results release, “Based on the increased demand visibility we are receiving from our customers, we expect another strong growth year for Applied Materials in 2027.”
Yet, equipment orders are discretionary, and a stock carrying a year-to-date gain of that size has a long way to fall whenever that spending is questioned. Policy adds another layer of risk, since China still made up a large share of Applied Materials’ revenue last quarter. Even after the pullback, Applied Materials shares hold most of their gain for the year, which leaves room for further profit-taking if spending plans shift.
Investors should track whether customer projects at the EPIC Center begin on schedule, since that work supports the bull case. A widening gap between the equipment trio and the iShares fund could signal deeper worries about fabrication budgets, while a narrowing gap could suggest the selling is fading.
Trading in Lam Research stock and KLA stock offers a useful cross-check, since both companies sell into the same fabrication budgets. Investors should keep their positions sized to that kind of volatility.

pages.title: Applied Materials vs. SK Hynix: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool

▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
The AI boom puts Applied Materials (AMAT -1.97%) and SK Hynix (SKHY -2.16%) at the center of the chip race. Choosing between the equipment giant and the memory leader depends on your goals for 2026.
Applied Materials provides the essential tools used to build semiconductors, while SK hynix produces the memory chips that store and move data. Both companies are critical to the global supply chain, yet they operate in different niches. This comparison explores their financial health and market positions to help you determine which stock better fits your strategy.
Applied Materials leads the materials engineering sector by providing the equipment and services required to deposit, shape, and analyze materials with atomic precision for chipmaking. It recently expanded its collaboration with Intel (INTC -0.37%) to advance AI technologies and maintains a strategic partnership with TSMC to meet growing foundry demand. Two specific partners account for approximately 19% and 15% of revenue, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, representing a growth of roughly 4.4% as the company benefited from increased demand for logic and foundry equipment. Net income for the period was approximately $7.0 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 24.7%. This figure reflects a slight decrease from the 26.4% net margin recorded in FY 2024, yet it remains significantly higher than the levels seen in FY 2023.
As of its October 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, calculated as total debt (short-term plus long-term) divided by shareholders' equity. The current ratio is roughly 2.6x, indicating the company can comfortably cover its short-term liabilities with current assets. Free cash flow, calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached nearly $5.7 billion for the fiscal year.
SK Hynix focuses on the memory side of the industry, producing the DRAM and NAND Flash components essential for modern data storage and processing. As the artificial intelligence boom continues to fuel demand for semiconductor stocks, the company is pursuing a "Full Stack AI Memory" strategy. This approach focuses on high-bandwidth memory and next-generation storage for data centers to capture a larger share of global digital infrastructure spending.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $72.5 billion, representing a massive growth of approximately 46.8% as the company capitalized on a recovery in memory prices. Net income for the same period was close to $32.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 44.2%. This performance is a sharp recovery from FY 2023, when the company reported a significant net loss during a memory market downturn.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2x, calculated as total debt (short-term plus long-term) divided by shareholders' equity. The current ratio is approximately 1.9x, indicating the company's ability to pay its immediate debts using its current assets. Free cash flow for the year totaled nearly $18.5 billion, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures.
Applied Materials faces significant risks related to export controls and trade regulations, particularly concerning shipments of advanced equipment to China. The company recently settled a $252 million penalty for unauthorized exports to Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation and remains under government scrutiny. Furthermore, its business is highly cyclical and sensitive to the spending plans of a small number of major chipmakers.
SK Hynix operates in the volatile memory market, where prices for products like DRAM can fluctuate wildly based on global supply and demand. It faces intense competition from rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology, which are also scaling up production for high-growth AI applications. If these competitors create a market glut, it could lead to lower prices and compress the company's net margin.
SK Hynix appears significantly cheaper based on future earnings estimates, while Applied Materials trades at a premium relative to sales over the past 12 months. Forward P/E measures price against future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio compares market value to sales over the past twelve months.
Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
When comparing Applied Materials and SK Hynix, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.
First, there's growth. Both companies are growing fast, but SK Hynix is a true outlier. It has averaged 50% year-over-year revenue growth over the last five years. In its most recent quarterly report, the company delivered a stunning 233% growth rate. Applied Materials, by contrast, has averaged 8% revenue growth, with its most recent report showing 25%.
Another factor to consider is each company's valuation. Here again, SK Hynix can claim an edge. On a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis, SK Hynix has a valuation multiple of 7x, while Applied Materials has a 41x multiple. In short, by this measure, SK Hynix is roughly 6 times cheaper than Applied Materials.
Last, there's profitability. When it comes to profitability, the comparison can get complicated. Overall, Applied Materials has delivered steady, solid profits. Its operating margin has averaged 30% over the last five years. SK Hynix, by contrast, has averaged around 21%. However, that average is dragged down by years of losses in 2023 and 2024. Since 2025, SK Hynix has maintained a higher operating margin than Applied Materials, and in recent quarters, it has soared to well over 50%.
In summary, it's appropriate for growth-oriented investors to give both of these stocks strong consideration. However, in a head-to-head matchup, SK Hynix comes out ahead due to its superior growth rate, lower forward P/E multiple, and excellent operating margin.

Broadcom vs. Applied Materials: Which Buybacks Are Actually Shrinking the Share Count?

Broadcom and Applied Materials both generate cash and repurchase shares, but shareholders ultimately own a fraction of a business. Our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade makes that distinction important: buyback spending is useful only in the context of issuance, the price paid and the cash needed to sustain growth. Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) offers custom silicon, networking and software exposure. Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) sells semiconductor-manufacturing equipment and services. They are different routes into AI-related investment, compared here on shareholder participation in cash growth.
Broadcom vs. Applied Materials: Which Buybacks Are Actually Shrinking the Share Count?
Close-up of Silicon Die are being Extracted from Semiconductor Wafer and Attached to Substrate by Pick and Place Machine. Computer Chip Manufacturing at Fab. Semiconductor Packaging Process.
A repurchase bill is not a net reduction
Broadcom spent $8.450 billion on repurchases over its first nine fiscal months. Yet weighted-average basic shares rose from 4.705 billion to 4.752 billion year over year, about 1.0%. Applied spent $1.177 billion over its first nine fiscal months, while weighted-average basic shares fell from 807 million to 794 million, about 1.6%.
The fiscal periods also differ slightly. They nevertheless show why dividing repurchases by market capitalization can overstate the ownership benefit: issuance and timing affect the actual denominator.
Applied delivered the more favorable net share-count direction in these reported periods. That does not prove its repurchases created more value. Buying overvalued shares can destroy value even when the number outstanding falls. Our Lam-Applied cash-coverage comparison tests a different prerequisite: whether payouts were supported by cash after investment.
Cash compensation and stock compensation both matter
Broadcom reported $6.287 billion of stock-based compensation in the nine-month cash-flow reconciliation; Applied reported $545 million. Stock compensation is added back in operating cash flow because it is noncash in that period, but it can dilute shareholders or require repurchases to offset issuance. It should not be mistaken for a costless source of cash.
Their nine-month operating cash after direct capital expenditure was $31.937 billion and $3.580 billion. As a conservative accounting-cost sensitivity, subtracting reported stock compensation leaves $25.650 billion and $3.035 billion. This is not GAAP cash flow or the cash actually needed to neutralize dilution; grant values, vesting and future repurchase prices differ.
If company-wide cash grew 10% while shares increased 1%, cash per share would rise about 8.9%. With shares falling 1.6%, the same cash growth would produce about 11.8% per-share growth.
At October 16 equity values, trailing cash after capital spending cost about 40 times for Broadcom and 58 times for Applied. Broadcom's lower multiple and stronger cash generation can outweigh modest dilution, while Applied's shrinking denominator cannot alone justify its price.
For investors weighing the chip-design alternative, our Nvidia-Broadcom comparison connects the cash-flow price with the growth assumptions behind each business.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders fell to 170 from 173 for Broadcom and to 137 from 138 for Applied. Fisher increased Broadcom shares 3%; Coatue reduced Applied shares 20%. Broadcom's September 30 short interest was 1.16% of float.
Applied currently shows the better net share-count direction. The lasting investment test is cash growth per share after competitive reinvestment, rather than the largest repurchase announcement or the smallest stock-compensation adjustment.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of AVGO and AMAT as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Applied Materials Cratered in The last 3 Months: One Wall Street Sell Side Firm Predicts it Will Nearly Double Within 12 Months
Applied Materials just posted its fifth consecutive earnings beat while the stock cratered 22% in three months, and at least one Wall Street firm thinks that disconnect points to one of the more compelling setups in the chip equipment sector…
Published October 14, 2026, 7:15am ET · 4 min read
This chart illustrates Applied Materials (AMAT) analyst ratings, price targets, and performance metrics, highlighting a 36.9% upside potential from its current trading price of $464.24. © 24/7 Wall St.
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT | AMAT Price Prediction) currently trades at $464.24, while Wall Street’s average price target stands at $635.33. That gap implies 36.9% upside.
Applied Materials builds the deposition, etch, inspection and packaging tools that chipmakers use to produce AI processors and high-bandwidth memory. Its latest quarter delivered revenue of $9.115 billion, up 24.8% year over year, and non-GAAP EPS of $3.50 against a $3.39 consensus. That was its fifth consecutive beat.
The business is accelerating while the stock falls, and investors need to know whether the market sees something analysts are missing.
An Investor Day Omission Deepened a 22% Three-Month Slide
Applied Materials declined to provide an industry spending forecast at its investor day, and shares fell 6.69% in a single session. Barron’s noted the stock was on pace to close lower for a sixth consecutive trading session. The one-week loss reached 12.45%, and the three-month decline stands at 21.98% from $595.06. Shares now sit 37.2% below their 52-week high of $738.88.
The pressure started earlier. Reuters reported that shares slipped after the August earnings report as an upbeat outlook failed to soothe investors seeking faster growth after a stellar run. Management also highlighted a hard constraint on the call: “It will be the availability of clean room at a high level that will determine what we can all ship next year.” With no spending forecast on offer, investors had to price that uncertainty themselves.
The weakness hit the whole group, but Applied took the most damage. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) fell 2.73% and KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) dropped 3.22% on the same day, while the S&P 500 slipped just 0.01%.
Analysts Keep Raising Estimates as the Stock Falls
Analysts are focused on to AI-driven demand that management says stretches years out. Applied expects leading-edge foundry logic, DRAM and advanced packaging to represent “around 80% of wafer fab equipment growth in 2026 and 2027,” and projects packaging revenue to grow “more than 70% in calendar 2026.” DRAM revenue, including HBM packaging, grew 52% year over year. Fiscal Q4 guidance calls for revenue of about $10.25 billion and non-GAAP EPS of roughly $4.02. Customer visibility now includes “some conversations now extending to 2030.”
Revisions point higher. The fiscal 2027 EPS consensus has rose to $18.4658 from $16.5279 90 days ago, and the January-quarter estimate drew 18 upward revisions in the past week with none lower. The top fiscal 2027 estimate reaches $21.77, which supplies the earnings math behind the most aggressive near-doubling calls by HC Wainwright, with its $900 target price. Ratings break down as 4 Strong Buy, 29 Buy, 7 Hold and no Sells.
Rising estimates coupled with a falling price signal multiple compression, and at 23x forward earnings the stock still prices in sustained growth. Analyst targets are 12-month opinions and carry no guarantee.
Chip Equipment Peers Fell Together, and Applied Fell Hardest
The semiconductor equipment group sold off as a pack, so Applied belongs to a broader falls. It has simply dropped further.
Lam Research lost 9.82% over the past week. The stock trades at $301.11, versus a $375.81 average target, implying 24.8% upside. Ratings show 4 Strong Buy, 25 Buy and 6 Hold with no Sells. Wall Street sees less upside here than for Applied.
KLA fell 6.82% over the week and trades at $184 versus a $232.77 target, implying 26.5% upside. Its 5 Strong Buy, 14 Buy and 10 Hold ratings make it the most carefully rated name of the group. Its upside also trails Applied’s.
Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) is an adjacent AI-infrastructure play that sells hard drives. It has fallen 32.4% over three months. The shares trade at $380.71 versus a $668.50 target, implying 75.6% upside, with 4 Strong Buy, 17 Buy and 5 Hold ratings. Melius Research has the highest target on the Street at $1,050.
Western Digital carries the largest implied upside of the group. Among direct equipment peers, Applied offers the widest gap to consensus.
An 81% Year-to-Date Gain Still Leaves the S&P 500 Far Behind
Applied trades at $464.24 against a consensus target of $635.33, implying 36.9% upside across 40 analysts. The three-month decline of 21.98% sits alongside a 1.7% one-month gain, showing the damage arrived in two sharp waves.
Year to date, Applied is up 81.29% while the S&P 500 has gained 14.1%. Over one year, the stock has returned 112.71% against 17.35% for the index. The 50-day moving average of $489.74 now sits above the share price, with the 200-day average at $435.51.
Applied Materials Bull and Bear Cases Hinge on the 2027 Spending Outlook
Shares look more compelling if DRAM and advanced packaging ramp as guided and fiscal Q4 lands near $10.25 billion. That keeps the $18.4658 fiscal 2027 EPS path intact and makes a forward multiple near 23x look reasonable for this growth rate. A clear 2027 spending outlook would also remove the uncertainty behind this week’s drop.
The bear case gains weight if clean room shortages cap shipments, export controls squeeze China sales, or the investor day silence signals a weaker 2027 than analysts model. China already declined to 28% of revenue from 35%.
On balance, the data leans positive. Estimates are rising, guidance points higher, and the stock trades 37.2% off its high. The missing forecast is a real yellow flag, so management’s 2027 outlook is the next data point to keep an eye on.

pages.title: ASML vs. Applied Materials: Which Chip-Equipment Stock Is the Better Buy? | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
Semiconductor manufacturers are planning huge expansions over the next few years to meet the booming demand for AI chips. Memory chipmakers hesitated to expand at first, but now have hundreds of billions of dollars worth of new facilities set to go into chip production starting next year. Meanwhile, the largest third-party chip manufacturer in the world, TSMC, has continuously raised its capital expenditure budget as it aims to keep up with demand.
While there are multiple ways to invest in the growing demand for semiconductor production, one of the best is to move up the supply chain to silicon wafer fabrication equipment makers. Two of the biggest companies in the space are ASML (ASML -0.99%) and Applied Materials (AMAT -1.97%). Both are excellent companies with strong competitive advantages, but if you can only choose one, which stock is worth buying today?
Image source: Getty Images.
Applied Materials: A diversified approach
Applied Materials holds a broad portfolio of equipment and maintains a very impressive market share across the group. Its deposition equipment (which adds conductive or insulating materials to a silicon wafer) is one of its fastest-growing businesses in 2026, even as it maintains a leading market share. The company is also seeing strong growth across etching, process diagnostics and control, and its thermals and treatments segments.
The diversified approach comes with a significant benefit. Applied Materials can sell combined offerings to customers by integrating different processes into a single piece of equipment. That can save its customers up-front costs as well as floor space, increasing production capacity. Over time, Applied Materials has come to work more closely with its customers, which has given it better insight into their needs.
Market capMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.$327.84B
Of course, maintaining a broad portfolio of market-leading equipment also requires significant investment in research and development (R&D). Applied Materials' R&D budget is significantly larger than its competitors' with much narrower product lines. That said, Applied Materials also earns revenue capable of supporting that R&D. Its operating margin of 31% is below that of competitors like KLA and Lam Research, but that's largely due to the lower-gross-margin profile of deposition equipment, which accounts for a larger share of Applied Materials' revenue.
In fact, the large R&D budget could ultimately benefit Applied Materials, as it enables the company to innovate quickly and stay ahead of competitors. Its leading position in deposition could enable it to gain market share in other equipment, especially through its integrated solutions. As a result, operating margin should expand over time, leading to very strong earnings growth.
ASML makes lithography machines that print circuits on silicon wafers. It's an absolutely dominant force with about 90% of the total market for lithography equipment and technological capabilities that are years, if not decades, ahead of the next-closest competitor.
That lead is crucial, especially in the current period of rapidly expanding production capacity. ASML's machines last for up to 30 years. That means competitors hoping to catch up to ASML will miss out on sales during the current investment cycle, while ASML benefits from a growing installed base to service each year. ASML is working to take advantage of the situation by expanding its own capacity by 30% next year and a further 30% in 2028.
Market capMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.$634.83B
The move should produce very strong earnings growth for the business as it sells more high-end machines, which carry higher margins and higher service revenue. Even memory chipmakers (which are much less technologically advanced than logic chipmakers) are looking to use ASML's most advanced equipment. The expanded scale should also support higher operating margins.
Which stock should you buy?
Both companies are set to experience very strong growth over the next few years as sales climb and margins expand. ASML's dominant position in lithography means it can charge premium prices for its equipment, limited only by its customers' ability to produce meaningful returns on the capital invested. With the rising prices for both memory and logic chips fueled by AI demand, that trend is working very much in favor of ASML.
However, Applied Materials has the opportunity to expand its market share of higher-margin equipment as manufacturers expand capacity over the next few years by cross-selling and integrating equipment across its broad portfolio. That could ultimately position it for much stronger revenue growth over the long run, as its share gains tend to be sticky. There's no room for ASML to increase its market share.
The two stocks trade for similar forward P/E ratios around 40 times expectations over the next 12 months. If you go out to 2028, ASML trades for 23 times analysts' earnings-per-share expectations for the year, while Applied Materials trades for 21 times expectations. Given Applied Materials' ability to maintain a higher growth rate over the long run after the current investment cycle, it looks like the better buy right now.

Applied Materials vs. ASML: Which Can Carry a Bigger Research Bill?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 5:56 PM CDT 3 min read
Keeping a semiconductor-equipment franchise valuable for ten years requires repeated invention. Our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade includes Applied Materials and ASML because both supply demanding manufacturing processes. Their latest results show different amounts of profit available to support the next research cycle.
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) reported $1.10 billion of research, development and engineering expense in its July quarter. ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML) reported €1.174 billion of research expense in its September quarter. Comparing their dollar budgets would require a currency conversion; comparing their operating burdens does not.
Innovation has to survive a weaker quarter
Applied's research expense represented 12.1% of its $9.115 billion revenue. ASML's represented 10.1% of €11.662 billion sales. Their reported operating incomes were $3.075 billion and €5.173 billion, respectively, after those expenses.
If each research bill increased 25% while everything else stayed unchanged, Applied's operating profit would fall 8.9%, against 5.7% for ASML. Each could absorb that isolated increase while remaining profitable. The exercise measures current funding capacity, not engineering productivity or the return on a particular project.
Research outlays are also only part of the investment requirement. Facilities, supplier capacity and working capital consume cash separately. Our TSMC-ASML capital-spending comparison shows why research expense alone cannot capture an equipment company's full expansion burden.
Different paths to the next technology cycle
Applied's EPIC partnerships are intended to shorten the path from materials research to manufacturing. That offers exposure to multiple process steps and advanced packaging. The risk is that a broad project portfolio consumes resources without producing enough profitable customer adoption. Announced collaborations do not establish future revenue.
ASML's lithography roadmap offers unusually important exposure to advanced chipmaking. Its October presentation described an initiative with TSMC for larger photomasks in High NA EUV. The intended productivity improvement remains a development objective, not proof of a completed commercial return. Customer readiness, system acceptance and export restrictions can delay monetization.
Applied's wider materials portfolio and ASML's lithography concentration are genuine alternatives. An investor can prefer breadth even when the specialist currently has the larger profit cushion.
Capacity and valuation are separate tests
At October 16 equity values, historical cash after capital expenditure cost about 58 times for Applied and 26 times for ASML. Those multiples are sensitive to investment and collection timing. ASML's latest operating cash included a large working-capital inflow, so its low historical cash multiple needs scrutiny rather than automatic endorsement.
Our Lam-Applied payout analysis tests how much cash remains available after investment and distributions. A company can afford research while still leaving shareholders little near-term cash.
Commercialization also needs access to customers.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders were 137 for Applied, down from 138, and 140 for ASML, up from 133. Coatue reduced Applied shares 20%; Fisher increased ASML shares 3%. ASML's September 30 short interest was 0.37% of float.
ASML currently has more operating capacity relative to its research bill. Applied's case rests on productive breadth and commercialization. The next evidence to watch is profitable adoption of new technologies, not simply a larger development budget or another partnership announcement.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of AMAT and ASML as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. If you are looking for an AI stock that is more promising than AMAT and ASML and that has 10,000% upside potential, check out our report about this cheapest AI stock.

How EPIC Center Launch Will Impact Applied Materials Stock
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 5:14 PM CDT 5 min read
Applied Materials has opened its US$5b EPIC Center in Sunnyvale, a 600,000-square-foot semiconductor equipment and process R&D hub that brings chipmakers, suppliers and universities into a shared cleanroom complex designed to speed commercialization of AI focused manufacturing technologies.
The EPIC Center's co-location of materials researchers, equipment engineers and chip production teams could reshape how Applied Materials converts AI related demand into higher value tools, services and long term customer relationships.
The next phase will center on how this EPIC Center collaboration model might influence Applied Materials' longer term investment narrative.
Spot 55 AI infrastructure stocks that could benefit alongside Applied Materials as capital pours into the tools and infrastructure behind AI focused chip manufacturing.
Applied Materials Investment Narrative Recap
The big picture with Applied Materials is simple. You need to believe that AI focused chip spending turns into demand for higher value tools, services and advanced packaging, and that the EPIC Center helps the business win a larger share of that work. The key near term catalyst is execution on AI linked orders and mix shift into richer segments rather than just chasing volume.
The fresh risk is that heavy EPIC and capacity investment, on top of flat gross margin guidance, keeps free cash flow conversion under pressure. The new center itself does not change that risk in the short run. If anything, it raises the bar on Applied Materials to prove that higher capex eventually feeds through to earnings quality instead of simply adding cost.
Among recent announcements, the extended collaboration with Intel around the EPIC Center looks most relevant. Both groups plan to work on next generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging, all of which tie directly into the AI manufacturing play that the new facility targets. That link matters for the catalyst many investors focus on, which is richer product mix and deeper process control content per wafer.
If Intel and other partners use EPIC to shorten learning cycles and qualify more tooling in leading edge nodes and 3D stacking, Applied Materials gains earlier visibility into customer roadmaps and potential pull through for its higher value segments. The flip side is execution risk. Any delay in getting these joint programs into high volume manufacturing, or weaker than expected adoption of new process steps, could leave the EPIC spend feeling heavy compared with nearer term earnings and cash generation.
Applied Materials' current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$58.5b and earnings of US$19.6b by 2029, based on an assumed 23.8% yearly revenue growth rate and an increase in earnings of about US$10.3b from US$9.3b today.

Applied Materials is Going Solid. Is its AI Growth Already Priced In?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:31 AM CDT 4 min read
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) has given investors more than an AI growth story by delivering the earnings necessary to support it. The stock generated a one-year total return of 79.4%, compared with 13.72% for the S&P 500. After such a rally, the question for investors is no longer whether Applied Materials is benefiting from semiconductor investment, but how much further its profitability can improve.
Yahoo Finance's September 17 valuation snapshot puts AMAT at 23.42 times forward earnings, compared with 23.92 in October 2025, and therefore provides a reference for examining whether the growth supporting the stock's valuation is sustainable.
In other news, we meticulously compiled a list of the best big name stocks to buy according to financial media, and there are nine stocks other than AMAT that rank in that list. Access the complete list for free here.
Applied Materials (AMAT) - Among Billionaire Steven Cohen’s Top 11 Dividend Stock Picks
Applied's third-quarter results offer more than encouraging sales figures. Revenue increased 25% year-over-year to a record $9.12 billion, while non-GAAP EPS climbed 41% to a record $3.50. More importantly, non-GAAP operating margin expanded from 30.7% to 34.0%. Earnings grew considerably faster than revenue, demonstrating that higher sales translated into stronger profitability. Read more about what Jim Cramer thinks about AMAT here.
The company's Semiconductor Systems division further illustrates that improvement. Revenue reached $7.04 billion, while its non-GAAP operating margin increased to 38.0% from 33.2%. This is particularly relevant for valuation because Applied is generating more operating profit from each dollar of segment revenue, rather than depending exclusively on additional equipment sales.
Read more about AMAT's investment case in our recently published article on ASML vs. Applied Materials: Which AI Chip-Equipment Stock Is the Better Buy?
Anyway, there is another dimension to the growth story for Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT). Applied Global Services generated $1.78 billion in quarterly revenue, compared with $1.46 billion a year earlier. Services provide a source of revenue alongside new equipment purchases, although their performance also depends on customer activity.
Management's latest ambitions extend further, as on October 13, Applied outlined plans to gain more than two percentage points of wafer-fabrication-equipment market share by 2030, while targeting non-GAAP gross and operating margins of approximately 54% and 40%, respectively. These are management targets, not achieved results, but they illustrate the additional profitability the company is pursuing. Which other big name stocks does the financial media favor? Access our complete list here for free.
We also shortlisted the best healthcare stocks to buy according to hedge funds. Check out the complete list here to make an informed decision.
The difficulty for investors is determining how much of that future improvement investors are already anticipating. The company reported in its fiscal Q3 2026 results that its latest non-GAAP gross margin was 50.4%, below management's longer-term 54% target through 2030. Reaching that level requires continued execution, and the current results cannot establish when or whether the target will be achieved.
In addition, the business is exposed to how much its semiconductor customers invest and when they place orders. The company itself identifies customer concentration, shifting capacity requirements, and trade restrictions among the uncertainties affecting future results. Semiconductor Systems still represents about three-quarters of revenue, so a weaker equipment-spending environment would matter even if services keep expanding.
Capacity planning adds another consideration for Applied Materials. Inventories increased to $6.56 billion at July's quarter-end from $5.92 billion in October 2025. Building inventory supports anticipated demand, but it also increases the importance of accurately forecasting customers' equipment requirements.
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) has demonstrated that AI-related demand can produce faster earnings growth and expanding margins, giving its valuation support beyond expectations alone. However, its exceptional share-price performance makes future execution increasingly consequential.
The real test is whether Applied can translate its ambitious market-share and margin targets into sustained earnings growth. Its latest results show significant progress, but investors must distinguish the profitability already achieved from the additional gains management expects to deliver.

Applied Materials, Inc. (AMAT) Is a Trending Stock: Facts to Know Before Betting on It
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 7:00 AM CDT 5 min read
Applied Materials (AMAT) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.
Over the past month, shares of this maker of chipmaking equipment have returned -7.9%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +1.5% change. During this period, the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry, which Applied Materials falls in, has lost 8.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?
While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.
Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.
For the current quarter, Applied Materials is expected to post earnings of $4.06 per share, indicating a change of +87.1% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged over the last 30 days.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $12.79 points to a change of +35.8% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has remained unchanged.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $18.27 indicates a change of +42.9% from what Applied Materials is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.
With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Applied Materials.
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for AMAT
Even though a company's earnings growth is arguably the best indicator of its financial health, nothing much happens if it cannot raise its revenues. It's almost impossible for a company to grow its earnings without growing its revenue for long periods. Therefore, knowing a company's potential revenue growth is crucial.
In the case of Applied Materials, the consensus sales estimate of $10.3 billion for the current quarter points to a year-over-year change of +51.4%. The $34.25 billion and $45.64 billion estimates for the current and next fiscal years indicate changes of +20.7% and +33.3%, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Applied Materials reported revenues of $9.12 billion in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +24.8%. EPS of $3.5 for the same period compares with $2.48 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $9 billion, the reported revenues represent a surprise of +1.31%. The EPS surprise was +3.55%.
The company beat consensus EPS estimates in each of the trailing four quarters. The company topped consensus revenue estimates each time over this period.
No investment decision can be efficient without considering a stock's valuation. Whether a stock's current price rightly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects is an essential determinant of its future price performance.
Comparing the current value of a company's valuation multiples, such as its price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), to its own historical values helps ascertain whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, whereas comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of how reasonable its stock price is.

pages.text:

Applied Materials Stock Fell 21% in 8 Straight Sessions. Here’s What Its 2030 Targets Mean for Shares
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 2:39 PM CDT 4 min read
Applied Materials Stock Fell 21% in 8 Straight Sessions. Here's What Its 2030 Targets Mean for Shares ©@Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva, @Jakub Pabis from Pexels via Canva
What Happened?
"We're not going to give a specific WFE forecast today," Applied Materials (AMAT) CEO Gary Dickerson told investors at the company's SEMICON West breakfast on Oct. 13, 2026. He followed it with "tremendous confidence" that computing demand would keep growing. Even so, reports from BigGo and Dow Jones tied the stock's extra decline to the missing number. Shares closed down 6.69% at $464.24 that day and fell to $430.01 by Oct. 15, an eighth straight losing session.
The sector was already sliding. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had dropped for six sessions by Oct. 13, and memory stocks fell hard that day after a report on China's ChangXin Memory. Lam Research (LRCX), KLA (KLAC) and ASML (ASML) lost 2.6% to 3.5%, about half of Applied's decline or less.
The 2030 Margin Math Does Not Depend on a WFE Number
The breakfast did deliver targets, laid out in Applied's investor relations materials: a 54% non-GAAP gross margin and a 40% non-GAAP operating margin by calendar 2030. CFO Brice Hill put the current gross margin at about 50%. TIKR's fiscal 2026 consensus shows an EBIT margin of around 33%.
Hill then gave the bridge. "We'll expect to get 4 additional points on the gross margin. And we will expect to achieve 200 to 300 basis points in operating leverage," he said. He credited AI automation in corporate functions for the second part. The pieces add up: around 33%, plus 4 points, plus 2 to 3 points lands near 40%.
He expects about 100 basis points of gross margin gain a year, though not in a straight line. He also said Applied is raising prices, partly to cover costs such as fuel and rare earths.
Services may be the most overlooked target. Applied Global Services generated $6.385 billion in fiscal 2025, and Applied targets more than $12 billion by calendar 2030. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon asked why connected chambers rising from 37,000 to 90,000 only yields mid-teens growth. Hill answered that the installed base grows 5% to 10% a year, and new products supply the rest.
Applied Materials Global Services Operating Revenue (TIKR)
A Cheaper Multiple, a Target Cut and the China Math
Since Jan. 25, 2026, Applied's NTM normalized EPS estimate has risen 83% to $17.61. Over the same stretch, its forward P/E ratio fell to 24.41x from 33.48x.
China is the clearest reason for caution. Head of Investor Relations Michael Sullivan said Applied could sell into 100% of China's equipment market in the early 2020s, then 90%, and "closer to 70%" in 2025. Hill said the 2030 share-gain target still assumes growth in restricted Chinese accounts under current trade rules. China supplied $8.529 billion of Applied's $28.368 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, about 30%.
Evercore ISI cut its target to $590 from $700 on Oct. 14 and kept an Outperform rating. Cantor Fitzgerald's C.J. Muse reiterated an $850 target on Oct. 13, about 34% above TIKR's $632.28 Street mean. TIKR shows 29 Buy, 4 Outperform, and 7 Hold ratings. Fiscal Q3 adjusted EPS of $3.50 beat estimates, but GAAP EPS of $3.17 missed the $3.44 estimate.
Applied Materials NTM Price / Normalized Earnings (P/E) (TIKR)
Applied Materials Advanced Valuation Model (TIKR)
The mid case is a scenario, not a forecast. It assumes around 15% annual revenue growth, a net margin near 33% and a slightly shrinking P/E. Applied's own targets point a little higher: a 40% operating margin taxed at management's estimated 15% rate leaves about 34%, before interest income.
Management expects leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging to supply about 75% of equipment spending growth through 2030. The main risk is uneven timing, with Hill flagging supply chain "pinch points that have to be managed." Margins above 54%, which Cantor considers conservative, are the upside. A spending pause that compresses the multiple before earnings catch up is the downside.
Applied reports fiscal Q4 results on Nov. 12. The Street expects about $10.30 billion in revenue and $4.06 in adjusted EPS, inside guidance of $9.75 billion to $10.75 billion.
Gross margin is the line to watch against management's 50.4% guide. Meeting it is the first data point on the road to 54%. A miss would weaken the 2030 bridge at its first step.

Wall Street Analysts Think Applied Materials (AMAT) Could Surge 39.39%: Read This Before Placing a Bet
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 7:55 AM CDT 4 min read
Shares of Applied Materials (AMAT) have gained 10.2% over the past four weeks to close the last trading session at $464.24, but there could still be a solid upside left in the stock if short-term price targets of Wall Street analysts are any indication. Going by the price targets, the mean estimate of $647.09 indicates a potential upside of 39.4%.
The average comprises 33 short-term price targets ranging from a low of $515.00 to a high of $900.00, with a standard deviation of $92.03. While the lowest estimate indicates an increase of 10.9% from the current price level, the most optimistic estimate points to a 93.9% upside. More than the range, one should note the standard deviation here, as it helps understand the variability of the estimates. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts.
While the consensus price target is a much-coveted metric for investors, solely banking on this metric to make an investment decision may not be wise at all. That's because the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable.
But, for AMAT, an impressive average price target is not the only indicator of a potential upside. Strong agreement among analysts about the company's ability to report better earnings than they predicted earlier strengthens this view. While a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't gauge how much a stock could gain, it has proven to be powerful in predicting an upside.
Zacks Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for AMAT
Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.
Here's Why There Could be Plenty of Upside Left in AMAT
Analysts' growing optimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher, could be a legitimate reason to expect an upside in the stock. That's because empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
For the current year, one estimate has moved higher over the last 30 days compared to no negative revision. As a result, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has increased 0.2%.
Moreover, AMAT currently has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), which means it is in the top 20% of more than 4,000 stocks that we rank based on four factors related to earnings estimates. Given an impressive externally-audited track record, this is a more conclusive indication of the stock's potential upside in the near term. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) stocks here >>>> .
Therefore, while the consensus price target may not be a reliable indicator of how much AMAT could gain, the direction of price movement it implies does appear to be a good guide.

AMAT Stock Has Doubled This Year: Analyst Trims Price Target But Sees Higher 2027 Sales, Profit
Morgan Stanley raised its 2027 revenue forecast for Applied Materials to $50.7 billion and its EPS estimate to $20.92, citing higher NAND demand and better margins.
KIOXIA will join Applied Materials' EPIC Center to collaborate on advanced memory structures, stacking, packaging and materials engineering.
AMAT stock doubled year to date, and retail traders see Micron's quarterly report, due on Wednesday, as a fresh catalyst.
Applied Materials (AMAT) shares jumped 5.2% on Tuesday, making the semiconductor equipment maker the top gainer on the Nasdaq-100 and pushing the stock to its highest level since Aug. 18, after Morgan Stanley raised its expectations for the company's 2027 financials.
In after-hours trading, the company announced a partnership with Japan's KIOXIA to develop next-generation memory technologies. The stock, however, dipped 0.2% in overnight trading following the announcement.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
Morgan Stanley Ups AMAT's 2027 Forecasts
Morgan Stanley on Monday cut its price target for AMAT to $563 from $642, which still signals a 25% upside, while maintaining an 'equal weight' rating. However, the research firm simultaneously raised its projections for Applied Materials' 2027 revenue and EPS, signaling stronger earnings expectations despite the lower valuation target.
Morgan Stanley raised the revenue forecast to $50.7 billion and EPS estimate to $20.92, driven primarily by expectations for higher NAND demand and improved gross margins.
Applied Materials said KIOXIA, a major supplier of flash memory and solid-state drives, will join its EPIC Center in Silicon Valley as an innovation partner.
The companies will work on advanced memory structures, multi-chip stacking, advanced packaging and materials engineering aimed at increasing memory density, bandwidth and energy efficiency for AI applications.
The announcement does not represent a newly disclosed equipment purchase by KIOXIA. Instead, KIOXIA will collaborate with Applied Materials on research and development at the EPIC Center to accelerate the commercialization of new memory and packaging technologies.
Applied Materials: AI Memory Opportunity
Applied Materials' $5 billion EPIC Center is designed to bring chipmakers, equipment companies, universities and other partners together to develop semiconductor processes and move them more quickly from research into high-volume manufacturing.
The center gives chipmakers earlier access to Applied Materials' technologies and the company said in August that its EPIC Center had expanded to 11 R&D engagements.
For investors, the KIOXIA tie-up reinforces the potential for AI-driven memory demand to translate into equipment spending. As memory architectures become more complex, manufacturers require additional process steps, materials and advanced packaging capabilities, potentially increasing the amount of semiconductor equipment required per wafer.
These developments come as semiconductor equipment stocks have gained significantly in 2026, despite a pullback from their June peaks, driven by expectations of elevated AI-related chip spending.
Applied Materials stock has doubled this year, while KLA Corp. (KLAC) is up 62.3% and Lam Research (LRCX) is up 90%.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AMAT dipped in recent days and was 'neutral' on Tuesday, with traders linking gains in AMAT and peers KLA Corp. and Lam Research to Micron's upcoming quarterly report.
"Bullish prelude to Micron's $MU future Earnings are already here. Semi equipment names related to Micron's capex - $AMAT $KLAC $LRCX were all trending down. But recently all of them together got above all moving averages and trending up," a trader said.
"Certainly a strong indication that Micron's sustained demand and earnings are going to be good."

Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT | AMAT Price Prediction) is now priced at $409.29. The average analyst price target stands at $627.83, meaning 53.4% upside.
Applied makes the deposition, etch and inspection tools used to build virtually every new chip. AI infrastructure demand drove fiscal third-quarter revenue to $9.12 billion, up 24.8% year over year. Management guided the current quarter to about $10.25 billion.
The most bullish firms, including H.C. Wainwright and Susquehanna, have $900 targets. Those sit about 119.9% above the current price. Consensus upside stands above 40%.
Investor Day Silence Turned a Pullback Into a 37% Rout
The biggest hit came at Applied’s investor day, when the company declined to provide an industry spending forecast. Shares fell as much as 9% intraday, and the stock lost 19.28% over the past week. Since the start of July, Applied has dropped 37.05%. That leaves it 44.6% below its 52-week high of $738.88.
The first signs showed after the August earnings report. Shares fell about 4% even though guidance beat consensus. Morgan Stanley summed it up: “AMAT’s earnings were good, but not great.” Peers fell about 4% on investor day, so sector weakness made a company-specific hit worse.
33 of 40 Analysts Rate It a Buy as Estimates Climb
Of the 40 analysts who cover Applied, 4 rate it Strong Buy, 29 rate it Buy and 7 rate it Hold. None rate it Sell. Estimates rose while the stock fell. The fiscal 2027 EPS consensus is $18.4672, up from $16.7456 90 days ago. Over the past 30 days, analysts made three upward revisions and no cuts. The stock trades at about 22 times that figure.
Management guided fourth-quarter EPS to about $4.02. DRAM revenue, including HBM packaging, grew 52% year over year. Packaging revenue should grow more than 70% in calendar 2026. Leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging should account for about 80% of equipment growth.
The $900 camp argues that Applied is well placed in tools for Gate-All-Around transistors, backside power and HBM packaging. CEO Gary Dickerson set the timeline on the earnings call: “Based on the unprecedented visibility we’re receiving from our customers, we expect another strong record year in 2027.”
Lam, KLA and Teradyne Sold Off Too, but Applied Fell Hardest
The whole group fell over the past week, but Applied fell the most.
Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) lost 14.74% to $263.94. Its average target is $375.81, meaning 42.4% upside. Twenty-nine of 35 analysts rate it Buy or Strong Buy.
KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) dropped 12.82% to $165.74. Its target of $232.77 meaning 40.4% upside. Analysts are more cautious here, with 10 of 29 at Hold.
Teradyne (NASDAQ:TER) slid 15.33% to $325. Its target of $446.47 meaning 37.4% upside, and 12 of 17 analysts are bullish.
Applied has the largest consensus upside in the group. All of these targets are estimates, and they could fall if spending expectations drop.
A 59.83% Gain This Year Survives the Drawdown
Applied trades at $409.29. The average target from 40 analysts is $627.83, meaning 53.4% upside. Targets often lag sharp price moves, so treat that number as one input among several.
Even after the drop, the stock is up 59.83% year to date. The S&P 500 is up 11.93%. Over one year, Applied shares are up 80.75%.
Applied Materials Looks Like an Overcorrection Worth Researching
Applied Materials’ upside case strengthens if DRAM and leading-edge logic deliver the second-half surge management promised and fiscal 2027 earnings land near the $18.4672 consensus. At a forward P/E of about 23, that growth looks undervalued.
The upside story weakens if the investor day silence means equipment spending is peaking. Management claims multi-year visibility yet held back an industry forecast. China fell to 28% of revenue from 35%, and the Other segment’s loss widened to $118 million. A slowdown in AI capex would pull targets down toward the share price.
The data leans positive. Estimates are rising while the share price falls. Applied’s upside is also the largest of any peer. The next earnings report and its 2027 outlook will test that view. As the demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to accelerate, investors often weigh the merits of equipment providers against those of chip designers. Choosing between Applied Materials (AMAT -1.97%) and Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%) requires a close look at two very different roles in the global supply chain.
Applied Materials provides the essential tools used to fabricate advanced chips, while Broadcom designs specialized silicon and infrastructure software. They are being compared because both are vital players in the artificial intelligence build-out, though they operate at different stages of the production cycle. This comparison evaluates their financial health and market positioning.
Applied Materials sells the complex machinery that other companies use to build chips, serving major foundries and memory makers. The expansion of global data centers has kept semiconductor stocks at the center of many growth-focused portfolios. Applied Materials maintains a highly concentrated customer base, with two customers accounting for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue in fiscal 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though it includes a deep partnership with Intel (INTC -0.37%) on next-generation manufacturing.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, an increase of 4.4% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $7 billion, which resulted in a net margin of close to 24.7%. This performance highlights the company's steady financial position in its latest annual report, filed for the period ending in late 2025.
As of its October 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.3. The current ratio, which indicates the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, was nearly 2.6. Free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, was approximately $5.7 billion for the fiscal period.
Broadcom provides a mix of specialized chips and infrastructure software. Its chips are essential for cloud data centers and high-end smartphones, while its software segment offers cybersecurity and cloud infrastructure. The company maintains major agreements including a $200 billion memorandum of understanding with Samsung and a $30 billion chip commitment with Apple (AAPL -1.00%).
In fiscal 2025, revenue grew by about 23.9% to nearly $63.9 billion. The company reported net income of approximately $23.1 billion for the year, resulting in a net margin of roughly 36.2%. This was a significant increase in profitability compared to the net income reported in the prior year.
As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.8, while its current ratio was nearly 1.7. Free cash flow reached roughly $26.9 billion for the year. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Applied Materials faces volatility inherent in the semiconductor industry and heavy geographic concentration. Nearly 89% of its revenue comes from outside the United States, making it sensitive to international trade shifts. Complex export controls, particularly regarding sales to China, remain a persistent challenge for the equipment maker. The company also paid a $252 million settlement in 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International.
Broadcom carries substantial indebtedness, which totaled nearly $67.12 billion as of late 2025. Its customer base is also highly concentrated, with a notable reliance on Alphabet for certain revenue streams. The company is navigating intense regulatory scrutiny, including antitrust challenges in the EU related to its VMware operations. Integration risks from large acquisitions and a legal dispute with AT&T (T +0.95%) also factor into its risk profile.
Broadcom is cheaper by forward P/E, which tracks future earnings estimates, while Applied Materials leads on P/S ratio, which measures market cap against 12-month sales.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Broadcom looks kind of expensive to me here. Applied Materials seems relatively boring; 4.4% growth isn't anything to write home about, but I think the valuation reflects that. On the other hand, Broadcom stock has outperformed Applied Materials by over 400 percentage points over the past 10 years, so its elevated valuation may also be justified.
On the other, other hand, smart investors know past performance is no indication of future results, and as a naturally conservative investor, I look at these companies' vastly different market caps and wonder which has the room for more growth. My guess is Applied Materials isn't going to knock your socks off, but it's outpaced the S&P 500 handily over the past 10 years. Furthermore, Broadcom seems closer to a ceiling than Applied Materials; the law of large numbers will make it harder for the former to keep posting those impressive revenue growth rates. I prefer Applied Materials.
